en: The platform cannot change what you use and, at the same time, keep in absolute secrecy what changed, when, why, what effect it had and which records make it possible to reconstruct the case. This duty is not a new law with a name of its own. It comes from the duty to inform, from good faith and from making it easier for consumers to defend their rights, which the law already provides for, and its purpose is to make the change verifiable.

When the platform changes the experience in a way that genuinely worsens, hollows out or diverts the function that led you to buy. That is the case with an item that, after an adjustment, is still in your inventory but has become so weak it no longer has a reason to exist, or a feature that let you do something and was taken away.

Some screen traps already have a name known worldwide, dark patterns. Examples include the box that comes pre-checked so you sign up for an extra service, the cancel button hidden in light gray and the warning that only a few units are left when that is not true.

The skin is different, because it only works inside a place you do not control. It goes through updates, balance adjustments, the end of events, catalog changes, changes in the game's currency and new policies. That is why the platform does not profit only from delivering the skin. It also profits by controlling access and time, that is, by charging for passage, for staying and for the predictability of a place that it governs itself.

At the same time, your progress, your status, your reputation and even your access depend on someone else's decisions, as happens with a worker who lives under conditions set by the boss. The word lumpenproletariat names those who work on the margins, without the rights of those who work. Applied here, it describes someone who is a consumer and, at the same time, labor, without the law seeing that second part.

The first objection is secrecy, which holds that requiring auditability would mean opening the code, handing over trade secrets and stripping the software of protection. The answer is that the legal order already accommodates limited forms of scrutiny that preserve the informational asset, such as sealed proceedings, restricted expert access, narrowly defined functional analysis and institutional oversight. Denis Borges Barbosa notes that sealing a case restricts third-party access to sensitive information, such as source code, and bars the opposing party from using it for purposes unrelated to the dispute. Reconciling protection of the asset with the need for verification is therefore nothing new.

The first objection is sentimentalism, the claim that protecting trajectory and reputation would mean protecting hurt feelings. But the injury is measured by the attribute objectively affected, and symbolic identity is a public, collectively verifiable position. The second is that history and records would be a data matter, foreign to consumption, but the administration of these elements is part of the very regime of enjoyment and interferes with the consumer's informational and biographical integrity. The third is the lack of full ownership. Article 24, item VII, of the Copyright Law answers it, because it shows that the legal order already accepts minimum duties of access to preserve the memory of an immaterial object under a third party's control, without making the consumer an author.

The case plays a supporting role, not a leading one, and appears in vignettes when a category needs to be stabilized or when it must be shown how the formal rule becomes enforcement practice. This use is kept in check by distinguishing three layers of normativity. The declared layer lies in the terms, policies and announcements. The norm in operation lies in the technical architecture, the interface flows and the concrete forms of enforcement and sanction, and it is there that the promise takes shape and much of the informational asymmetry is produced.

The disputed norm arises when the first two clash, because enforcement reveals what the text left unclear, because the text serves as an alibi or because a unilateral change shifts the balance without the consumer knowing what was altered. Keeping them apart prevents confusing statement with enforcement, promise with delivery and controversy with mechanism. The case has limits. The design focuses on this ecosystem, in its computer and mobile versions (the latter called Wild Rift), within a defined time frame and using public sources, and this choice neither maps variations by platform, national market or technological generation nor supports statistical inference. The reflection, therefore, is not about League of Legends as an isolated cultural object but about the regime of the immaterial object of consumption it contains.

The reading is not a full exegesis but a targeted extraction along four axes, namely how the object and the performance are qualified, the powers of unilateral modification and their triggers, the justification and allocation of risk, and the promises of compensation, refund and restoration. It also looks for the sanctions and appeal channels that exist and the duties of information that apply when something is altered, punished or restricted. For software, the period of technical validity, update cycles, discontinuation and support are included. The version in force is read and preserved as captured, and an earlier version is read only when there is a verifiable public record of it.

Platform consumption tends to be organized around a business model that extracts value from control of access, from manufactured scarcity and from the consumer's own presence, and this model explains supplier conduct that reading a clause in isolation cannot reach. Read with Varoufakis, Dowbor and Marx, the model gives the jurist conditions of attribution, and not a condemnation of the market.

The first objection is that the contract authorizes the change. The terms do normalize mutability and stabilize the scenario, by treating content as a revocable license and allowing alterations, but abusive teleology is not reducible to the contract, and contractual elasticity does not solve the problem when the offer built the attribute into the core of the good. Private autonomy, moreover, does not authorize organizing enjoyment on foundations structurally incompatible with good faith, balance and controllability. The second is that nothing was false, the text is not scandalous and the service remains available. The answer is that the CDC requires neither literal falsity nor scandalous text in order to react.

The price makes the shift visible. An Ultimate skin costs 3,250 RP, the game's paid currency, while the Exalted one is obtained through draws of 400 RP each, guaranteed only on the eightieth, which sets a ceiling of 32,000 RP, about 9.85 times more. At official prices in Brazil, the difference in reais is even more striking, and the amounts serve as a demonstration, without fixing a single price across all possible combinations. The jump is illustrative evidence that luxury, in this arrangement, is produced mainly by signs and by administered access. The observation matters for reading the promise, because in traditional markets the qualification of luxury presupposes a recognizable backing of superiority capable of sustaining the implicit expectation of quality and of distinction proportional to the price.

The first limit concerns persuasion. Economic activity has its own persuasive function, and control of the offer does not work as abstract repression of advertising, but as control of the promise in environments of governed enjoyment. The second concerns relevance. Informational adequacy is assessed by the elements that relevantly condition the formation of expectation, the preservation of enjoyment and the possibility of contestation, and there is a materially controllable offer wherever prior communication relevantly shapes the reading of the object, the perception of value and adhesion. The third concerns the symbolic. The contribution of the simulacrum does not lie in treating consumption as illusion, and the problem does not lie in desiring, fantasizing or attributing symbolic value to the object. The fourth concerns possibility. The consequences of anticipation are always possibilities, since unlawfulness may lie in the articulation and frustration may be a relevant inadequacy, so that a calendar, an event or a random draw does not become abusive merely by existing.

The first objection is that the consumer accepted the terms. The answer lies in the structure of the law of the platform, in which the contract is only one of the layers, so that, when the supplier organizes by design and enforcement the conditions of access, permanence and sanction, legal control cannot remain trapped on the contractual surface. Moreover, the precariousness of enjoyment cannot be naturalized by the mere invocation of contract, license, innovation or the global scale of the service.

The first objection is that only a service is provided, or only a license granted. The answer is that these formulas are not enough to naturalize the precariousness of the bond, and that bringing it back to the immaterial product does not deny the provision, which appears as the way of sustaining the object. Without the concept, the platform would always win by writing its own dictionary.

Four objections are usually raised against these duties. The first is secrecy, which holds that verifying the effects of supply would expose trade secrets and know-how, the English word for reserved technical knowledge. Barbosa supplies the answer. The know-how contract makes the supplier master of it only as between the parties, through contractual arrangement and not through sovereignty enforceable against everyone, and protecting the secret depends on the intent to keep it being regulated by obligations and on the confidential content being concretely defined. Where enjoyment, restoration or challenge are affected, confidentiality coexists with a minimum duty to make reviewable whatever the supplier intends to raise against the consumer. The supplier may protect its secret, but it may not use the word as fog to place what it does to enjoyment beyond challenge. The chapter on auditability shows the tools that allow verification without exposing the asset.

The second objection, a related one, holds that any minimum transparency would hollow out intellectual property, especially for software. It does not, because what the social function rejects is the use of the program's protection as an absolute barrier to scrutiny of the effects of supply, not the protection itself. The third is the appeal to system necessity. For Miragem, clauses or practices that give the supplier unilateral control so intense that it diminishes or eliminates the usefulness of the consumer's interests are substantively abusive. When governance rests on software, the platform tends to present as a system necessity what is, strictly speaking, a choice about how to manage supply.

The first objection, and the most corrosive, is the claim that the consumer has not proved it, which turns the consumer's lack of access into absence of proof of the right itself. In these environments, the absence of proof may reflect the supplier's governance arrangement more than any weakness of the claim, and the law cannot accept the platform administering at once the enjoyment, the narrative of the event and the conditions under which it can be verified.

The limit is also clear. What emerges from the models is not the conclusion that the IOC would serve for almost everything, and controllability does not depend on freezing innovation, imposing absolute transparency or turning the platform into a quasi-state entity. It depends on bringing private governance back to verifiable standards of intelligibility, evidence, equivalence and correction, against the naturalization of precariousness as the ordinary way of organizing the consumer's experience.

The first objection is complexity, according to which specific relief would be impracticable in a technical and continuously changing environment. This is an undue reduction, because the architecture of the environment cannot serve as an automatic excuse for downgrading remedies. The ninth guideline reinforces the point by recalling that control does not require the judge to become an engineer of the system.

The case that shows the political rationality of design is the balancing of League of Legends. The meta, short for metagame, is the set of dominant strategies and optimal choices stabilized in a given period, produced and corrected by buffs, which deliberately increase the power of a character, item or ability, and by nerfs, which reduce it. Buffs and nerfs are no mere accessory to the game but the means by which the ecosystem defines, in regular cycles, which characters and strategies remain viable and which fall, for a period, to suboptimal choices. The patch operates there as a norm in operation, because it reconfigures the competitive utility of assets, redistributes frequency of use and alters the real cost of staying. The update makes functional obsolescence an ordinary component of enjoyment, since what was learned, mastered and chosen can be downgraded within weeks by unilateral technical decision.

The case does not conclude that balancing is unlawful or that the company acted wrongly. Balancing is a regular exercise of governance, publishing the notes deserves praise, and the analysis requires no subjective intention. What it establishes is that the change is a decision with criteria, dates and effects, and can therefore be reconstructed and criticized. The legally decisive question then becomes which purposes were built into the architecture and which conditions of auditability make that choice open to criticism. If the alteration downgrades the functional and symbolic value that motivated the purchase, the examination depends on reconstructing what changed, the subject of the chapter on open auditability, and on measuring what was preserved, the subject of the chapter on functional value equivalence.

The first objection is that the change is just the normal working of the software, a tweak, an update or a balance pass. But this industry language hides the normative core under engineering vocabulary, because when the platform unilaterally alters a rare cosmetic item or redesigns a character, it determines by code the material conditions of enjoyment and the way the good will be recognized and compared in the social world of the game. If the alteration lowers the functional and symbolic value that motivated the acquisition, the problem stops being user nostalgia and becomes an architectural redefinition of the content delivered, with a direct effect on auditability and attribution, which remain here as a horizon, with no conclusion of abusiveness.

The label aggregates technical fragility, informational deficit, behavioral manipulation, algorithmic opacity, technological exclusion and economic asymmetry, and, by condensing so many layers, it stops indicating which one matters in each case, so that proof is dispersed and the remedy oscillates between abstraction and casuistry. The expressions electronic, virtual or technological vulnerability reveal the perception of a new problem, but they help locate where it happens and say less about how it is produced.

The first objection is psychologization. But semiotic vulnerability does not describe lesser individual discernment or subjective susceptibility. It describes the objective way in which the environment organizes language, visibility, comparison and proof, and it is neither a moral judgment about whoever did not read nor an explanation by impulse or addiction. The neighboring objection, of moralism against the symbolic or against advertising, has a similar answer, because the problem is not desiring the object or attributing symbolic value to it, but the expectation organized toward an image that the regime of supply does not sustain.

It is not a confession, but it shows the environment narrating itself as culture. And it shows that the law of the platform also governs through plot, style, character and performance, and not only through contract, code and screen.

When the change hollows out your place in the app, it may be possible to ask for the records to be preserved and disclosed. It may also be possible to ask for restrictions to be explained in a way that can be checked and for the penalty criteria to be reviewed. And you may be able to ask for clarity on how requests are handed out and for what was degraded to be restored.
Ordinary frustrations and normal changes to the service are left out. The loss needs to be significant and persistent, and it must be possible to describe it by verifiable criteria.

You pay the same as before but get less, because the service lost features, tightened limits, got slower or started demanding more to deliver the same thing. The name and the price stayed the same, and what shrank was the delivery. Brazilian consumer law treats as void any change the company makes on its own to the content or quality of what it sells.

The response prioritizes restoring access, reversing sanctions, preserving history, equivalent functional substitution and adjustments to governance. Compensation remains possible and plays an important role, including for non-pecuniary damages, but not as an automatic response. When the harm reveals a repeatable pattern, regime correction is warranted, with injunctive relief, structural measures and collective measures.

Qualification has effects on two levels. It prevents control from being neutralized by the claim that there is merely a service or merely a content license. And it redefines the reading of the Brazilian Consumer Protection Code (CDC), which now takes as its starting point enjoyment as a governed relationship, without denying the relevance of the contract. The service dimension does not disappear, because it appears as a way of sustaining, updating and shaping the object itself. The old question of product or service, framed as mutually exclusive, loses much of its analytical usefulness.

Change, in itself, is not unlawful. The problem begins when it significantly degrades, empties or diverts the function that justified the acquisition. The criterion is not reduced to technical performance or to isolated attributes. It looks at the role of the object in the acquired experience, its utility in the ecosystem, its place in relationships and, when it objectively and recognizably forms the core of the acquisition, its symbolic dimension.
